svg.data-weight-configured-scope: fully configured using all card slots and three power trays
svg.data-power-modules-v2: Version 2 power system - up to twelve AC power modules per system, four per tray
svg.data-power-modules-v3: Version 3 power system - up to nine AC power modules per system, three per tray
svg.data-power-ac-redundancy: AC power modules operate in N+N redundancy mode
svg.data-cooling-path: front-to-rear; inlet at the bottom front, exhaust at the upper rear
svg.data-fan-trays: two, FT0 over FT1, fitted from the REAR
svg.data-air-filter-location: three filters on the front of the RP and FC card cage

The 10 slot bays are EMPTY; fabric, rp are populated. Enough to power on and reach the box, which is the question most people ask first and the one `default` used to answer with whatever the drawing happened to be populated with.","kind":"base","source":"derived - built from the group roles rather than from a vendor bundle: every bay whose group is `service` or `management` keeps its seat, every `traffic` bay takes a blank. This vendor publishes no base configuration for this chassis, so the library defines one. Where a vendor DOES publish one, follow it instead and say so here."}},"description":"Cisco ASR 9912 Router - 30 RU, and the first chassis in this family with TWO card cages on one face. Ten vertical line card slots sit above a second cage of nine positions carrying two route processors flanking seven fabric cards, with three power shelves below. The two fan trays are fitted from the REAR, which the guide marks on the figure itself. Modelled as a bare cage with every card position a real bay.","format":1,"gaps":[{"note":"Cisco publishes no chassis-level power draw for any ASR 9000. Table 14's "Power Dissipation" row says only "Use the Cisco Power Calculator ... to estimate the maximum power distribution", so the chassis total is whatever its occupants sum to. Recorded in provenance as no-chassis-power-figure since the family was modelled; scoped here so a comparison can tell this apart from a figure nobody has looked for","reason":"vendor-silent","scope":["fact:peak-power-w","fact:typical-power-w"],"wanted":"a chassis-level maximum and typical draw from Cisco, or confirmation that the Power Calculator is the only answer the vendor will give","what":"chassis-power-figure"},{"note":"THESE BAY DIMENSIONS WERE GROWN TO MEET A COMPONENT AND ARE NOT MEASUREMENTS. Each was set by taking the size of a card the bay accepts, because a fit check reported the bay as too small. On this chassis: 42.67 on 10 bays - a9k-4hg-flex, 42.67 thick 403.10 on 10 bays - the 5th-generation envelope, 403.10 long The danger is specific and it is why they are listed rather than left to look like geometry. A fit check compares a bay to a component and NEITHER of them to the world, so it is satisfied by both being wrong together exactly as easily as by both being right. Every mismatch resolved by moving one side removes the signal without adding any truth, and once resolved nothing will flag it again. These are the entries where that happened, so the record survives the check going quiet. What IS independently grounded and is not in this list: the cage extents, measured off the stencil and confirmed on several chassis by printed slot labels or a card guide rail; the slot pitch; the 395.70 fourth-generation envelope, which is Cisco's own "includes ejector bracket/lever" figure; and the shapesheet sizes for the power modules and fan trays. The ejector arithmetic that explains why a bay legitimately exceeds its cage opening - 355.60 against 395.70, 40.10 mm - is also sourced, and it justifies the SHAPE of these numbers without justifying any particular one of them.","reason":"needs-drawing","scope":["slots"],"wanted":"a dimensioned figure giving the clear opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would replace every reconciled figure above with a measured one","what":"bay-extents-reconciled-rather-than-measured"},{"note":"A THIRD LINE OF EVIDENCE ON THE ~428 mm CONTROL CARDS, derived rather than asserted, and it comes from parts that have nothing to do with the question. The vertical space available to a card is bounded by whatever structure sits above and below its cage, and on this chassis that space measures the figure recorded in card-envelope-headroom below. A card envelope larger than that cannot be installed whatever any data sheet says, because something else is already there. Applied across the family:
 ASR 9010 399.96 mm between the cable management tray and the card guide bar
 ASR 9910 421.79 mm between the tray band and the front air intake
 ASR 9922 420.30 mm between the tray band and the fan band
 ASR 9912 439.21 mm - does NOT exclude 428.5, so this chassis is silent on the question
 ASR 9906 unbounded above in the model, so no constraint is derivable
Three of the five independently exclude a 428.2-428.5 card. That is a separate argument from the slot pitch and from the ejector arithmetic, and it agrees with both. THE 9912 DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT and is recorded as silent rather than as agreement - a constraint that fails to bite is not evidence either way, and reporting it as if it were would manufacture support. The 9010's 399.96 also sits 3.14 mm under the 403.10 fifth-generation envelope its bays now carry, which is a smaller open question of the same kind.","reason":"sources-disagree","scope":["slots"],"wanted":"a figure dimensioning the clear vertical opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would turn all of this from derived to measured","what":"neighbour-constraint-excludes-the-control-card-length"},{"note":"THE SECOND AXIS OF THE SAME CONFLICT, and it makes the first one much harder to explain away. The RSP-880 family is published at 428.5 mm on its long axis. Two Cisco statements fix what a line card measures on that axis in this family: Table A-10 of OL-17500-09 gives the original-generation card 14 in (355.60 mm) with NO qualifier, and the 4th-generation data sheets give 15.58 in (395.70) explicitly "including ejector bracket/lever". The 40.10 mm between them is the ejectors, about 20 mm each end - which is also why a bay declared at the 395.70 envelope is legitimately longer than the cage opening it sits in. Against that, 428.50 does not reconcile. Subtract the same 40.10 of ejector and the plate would still be 33.45 mm longer than this chassis's measured cage - a cage independently confirmed to 0.65 mm by Table A-10's own 355.60. So BOTH published RSP-880 dimensions, 46.0 thick and 428.5 long, are irreconcilable with a cage that two unrelated sources agree on. That is why the bays were NOT inflated to hold it. Building five chassis around a pair of numbers that contradict the only independently confirmed dimension in the family would put the error into the geometry instead of into the record. The accepts keep the RSP-880 where Cisco names it; the bays stay at what the cage and the reconcilable envelopes allow.","reason":"sources-disagree","scope":["slots"],"wanted":"the RSP-880's plate dimensions as distinct from whatever 46.0 x 428.5 measures, or a photograph of an RSP-880 beside a line card","what":"rsp880-length-also-exceeds-the-cage"},{"note":"Cisco's RSP-880 and RSP880-LT data sheet gives "Height: 1.81 in. (4.60 cm)", i.e. 46.0 mm, and names the ASR 9006, 9010, 9904, 9906 and 9910 as the chassis they are the system processor for. THAT WIDTH EXCEEDS THE MEASURED SLOT PITCH ON EVERY CHASSIS IN THE FAMILY:
 9010 44.33 9906 43.42 9910 43.78 9912 44.06 9922 44.06
and three of those pitches are measured from PRINTED SLOT LABELS or a card guide rail with a spread of 0.11 to 0.20 mm - among the best-supported numbers in this library. A card cannot be thicker than its slot, so 1.81 in is not the seating width; it is most likely taken over the ejector levers, the same way Cisco's line card "Width" is stated as "includes ejector bracket/lever" elsewhere. The accepts lists keep the RSP-880 family where Cisco names it, because a compatibility claim is Cisco's to make. The bays are sized to what the measured opening can hold. So a reader will find a bay narrower than a component it accepts, and that is a RECORDED CONFLICT between two sources rather than an oversight - the alternative was to inflate five chassis' geometry to fit one published number that three independent pitch measurements contradict.","reason":"sources-disagree","scope":["slots"],"wanted":"the RSP-880's seating width as distinct from its over-ejector width, or any Cisco statement of an ASR 9000 slot pitch","what":"rsp880-width-exceeds-every-measured-pitch"},{"note":"cisco/a99-sfc3@1 carries power-draw-max-w 340, and that figure is the ASR 9922's. Table 23 of b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf lists the SAME part number twice with different figures scoped by chassis - "A99-SFC3 Card (ASR 9922)" at 320/330/340 W across the three ambients, and a separate ASR 9912 row at a lower number. These are two scopes rather than two answers: the same card draws less in this chassis than in the 9922. A chassis total built from the component here is therefore CONSERVATIVE - it over-counts each of the seven fabric cards - which is the safe direction but is not the right number. The component cannot carry both without a chassis-scoped mechanism, which the library does not have; casa/c100g records the same species of problem for paired modules.","reason":"sources-disagree","scope":["fabric"],"wanted":"a per-chassis power scope on a component contract, or a separate PID for the 9912 variant","what":"fabric-card-power-is-scoped-to-the-9922"},{"note":"Three power shelves are drawn as single openings rather than four module openings each. Figure 23 numbers them M0 to M3 per shelf and Table 15 gives "Version 2 power system: Up to twelve AC power modules per system, four per tray" - so twelve, and the count is not in doubt. The boundaries are: the master draws all three shelves populated, so scanning returns module detail rather than separators. The shelves' vertical extents here are estimated from the band below the RP/FC cage rather than measured off separator rules, which is weaker than everything else in this file and is why they are cutouts and not bays.","reason":"needs-drawing","scope":["front"],"wanted":"a figure showing the power shelves empty, or a dimensioned front elevation","what":"power-module-openings"},{"note":"THE BOTTOM IS THE ONLY FACE OF THIS CHASSIS WITH NO SOURCE, and it is not a gap in this file's research. There is no bottom view of ANY ASR 9000 chassis anywhere in the 78-document intake: every figure caption in all 65 PDFs was searched for "Bottom View", "underside" and "bottom of the chassis", and the result is zero hits. That is a fact about how Cisco documents a rack chassis rather than about this model - a face that sits on rack rails and is never serviced gets no figure. The face is SIZED correctly from Table 13, so a rack elevation and the 3D box are the right shape; what it lacks is any statement of what is on it. Nothing is invented to fill it, and no region is added naming the absence, because a check passed by annotating that you have nothing is worse than a check failed honestly. THIS HOLDS THE CHASSIS AT CAPABILITY 2. Front, rear, top, left and right all now carry sourced content; the bottom alone does not, and level 3's implementation requires content on all six. The written design asks only that six faces be "present, sized, and mutually consistent", which this file satisfies - the content requirement comes from `_has_content`, which was written for level 1. See working/notes/deliberately-empty-faces.md.","reason":"vendor-silent","scope":["bottom"],"wanted":"a bottom elevation, a photograph of the underside, or a way for a view to declare itself deliberately empty so that empty-by-verification counts where empty-by-omission does not","what":"bottom-face-is-undocumented-family-wide"}],"groups":{"fabric":{"attrs":{"redundancy":"6+1","redundancy-note":"6+1 - b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide, "Fabric Switchover": "In the Cisco ASR 9922 Router and Cisco ASR 9912 Router, fabric switching across the RP and line cards is provided by a separate set of seven OIR FC cards operating in 6+1 redundancy mode. Any FC card can be removed from the chassis, power-cycled, or provisioned to remain unpowered without impacting system traffic. All FC cards remain active unless disabled or faulty." So the spare is a working plane and not a standby card. "Fabric Controller Card" in the same guide gives the partly-populated case: five FCs are 4+1, all seven are 6+1"},"index-origin":0,"physical-context":"NetworkingDevice","role":"service","term":"FC"},"grounding":{"index-origin":1,"role":"furniture","term":"Point"},"power-modules":{"attrs":{"redundancy":"n+n","redundancy-note":"n+n on AC, n+1 on DC - the AC power trays provide N+N redundancy and the DC power trays N+1 (Overview and Reference Guide, Power System). The form here is the AC one"},"index-origin":0,"physical-context":"Power Module","role":"service","term":"PM"},"rp":{"attrs":{"redundancy":"1+1","redundancy-note":"1+1 - b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide, "Stateful Switchover": "The RSP/RP cards are deployed in 'active/standby' configurations. Stateful switchover (SSO) preserves state and configuration information if a switchover to the standby RSP/RP card occurs." Unlike the RSP chassis in the series, no fabric rides on this card: "Functional Description" puts the route processor functions on the RP and the switch fabric on the FC cards"},"index-origin":0,"physical-context":"NetworkingDevice","role":"service","term":"RP"},"slots":{"index-origin":0,"physical-context":"NetworkingDevice","role":"traffic","term":"Slot"}},"kind":"device","manufacturer":"Cisco","maturity":"modelled","model":"ASR 9912","name":"asr-9912","portfolio":{"family":"Aggregation Services Router","line":"Service Provider","series":"ASR 9000 Series"},"provenance":{"air-filter":"datasheet - Table 17, b-asr9k-hardware-installation-guide.pdf p228: "Cisco ASR 9912 Router - Three air filters on the front of the RP and FC card cage". THREE filters, on the FRONT, which is unlike every other chassis in the family - the 9006 and 9904 put theirs on the right side and the 9010, 9906 and 9910 underneath a cage. Not modelled as bays; no figure dimensions them","airflow":"datasheet - "Cisco ASR 9912 Router: Front-to-rear cooling path. The inlet is at the bottom front of the chassis, and the exhaust is at the upper rear", b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf p3740","bay-sizing":"the bays are sized to the COMPONENT envelope, 41.4 x 395.7, and POSITIONED on the measured label centres. The 2.66 mm between that envelope and the 44.06 measured pitch is the card guide between slots, which is chassis structure rather than part of the bay. This follows the team's arbitration that a module's size is the slot envelope and that a bay and its occupant must carry the same size so the two can be checked against each other. NOTE FOR HARMONISING LATER: the ASR 9006 and ASR 9010 committed earlier size their bays to the cage OPENING instead, which predates that ruling and should be brought into line","bottom-face":"datasheet - the bottom is NOT featureless after all, and the feature is the one thing every footprint figure dimensions. Figure 14 dimensions 22 in (55.88 cm) from the rear. The rack mounting flange is a vertical plate spanning the chassis height, so it intersects the BOTTOM plane as well as the top and appears on this face as a line across the width at that depth. That is a real dimensioned feature rather than an annotation of absence, which is the distinction that matters here - an earlier revision of this file said the bottom was unreachable without inventing something, and that was wrong. What remains true is that no BOTTOM VIEW of any ASR 9000 chassis exists in the 78-document intake; what this face carries is a feature dimensioned in a TOP-down figure whose geometry the bottom necessarily shares. Positions are given from the REAR, which is how the figures dimension them","calibration":"measured - gate 1 passed. Calibrating x on 482.6 mm (the 19.0 in rack face) and y on Table 13's 1333.5 mm independently gives 0.20134 and 0.20144 mm/px, agreeing to 0.05 percent","card-compatibility":"datasheet - the per-card datasheets carry a "Chassis compatibility" row. c78-743580, the 5th Generation High-Density Multi-Rate data sheet, says of A9K-20HG-FLEX-SE/-TR and A9K-8HG-FLEX-SE/-TR: "Compatible with the Cisco ASR 9006, ASR 9010, ASR 9904, ASR 9906, ASR 9910, ASR 9912, and ASR 9922 chassis". This chassis is named, so those four are in every line card bay. Cards whose rows omit the 9912 are deliberately absent","card-envelope-headroom":"derived - 439.21 mm of clear vertical space between the structure above this card cage and the structure below it, measured off this chassis's own committed geometry. Any card envelope larger than that cannot be installed regardless of what its data sheet states. Used as a check on the control-card lengths, not as a source for the bays","card-orientation":"datasheet - stated directly, and it had been an inference until now. The Overview and Reference Guide's "Chassis Slots" section (b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf p17) names every chassis in the family and gives the ejector position as the tell: "Cisco ASR 9912 Router: All RP, FCs, and LCs are front-facing and mounted vertically, with ejector levers and captive screws at the top and bottom of each card". A bay therefore places a card component unrotated. Only the ASR 9006 and ASR 9904 are horizontal; the 9010, 9906, 9910, 9912 and 9922 all stand their cards up, including the 21 RU 9010. This section supersedes the three-way inference an earlier revision rested on - the slot figures, Figure 2's "four on each side" callout and the measured cage aspect - all of which agreed with it.","chassis":"datasheet - Table 13, b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf p130. ASR 9912: chassis height 52.5 inches (133.4 cm), chassis width 17.6 inches (44.7 cm) with "19.0 inches (48.3 cm) including chassis rack-mount flanges and front doors", chassis depth 25.7 inches (65.2 cm), "29.4 inches (74.7 cm) including the cable management system" and "30.1 inches (76.4 cm) including cable management system and front doors". Modelled as the BODY, 447.0 x 1333.5 x 652.0 mm, taking the bare depth. This row gives 17.6 and 19.0 on separate lines, which is what showed the ASR 9910's row has its flange phrase attached to the wrong number","compliance":"datasheet - data_sheet_c78-501767.pdf series compliance list, transcribed as printed","electrical":"datasheet - Table 15 (AC) and Table 16 (DC), pp132-135, ASR 9912 columns only","environmental":"datasheet - Table 14, p131. The 9912 is in the narrower short-term group, 23 to 122 degF (-5 to 50 degC), with the 9010, 9910 and 9922","fabric-and-rp":"datasheet - the seven FC positions accept cisco/a99-sfc3@1, which Table 23 names as an ASR 9912 part in its own right. The two RP positions accept the RP3 pair; the ASR 9900 Series Route Processor 3 data sheet is the source for the part and Figure 23 for the positions. THE FABRIC CARD'S POWER FIGURE IS SCOPED AND MUST NOT BE READ OFF THE COMPONENT HERE - see gaps","first-generation-fabric-accepted":"datasheet - the fabric bays gain this chassis's first-generation switch fabric card, placed on the component's own attrs.chassis, which names exactly one chassis. That single-chassis declaration is why it can be added without a compatibility row: the part says where it goes","four-hg-flex-accepted":"datasheet - the A9K-4HG-FLEX and A99-4HG-FLEX pairs added to the line card slots, and each is placed on ITS OWN declared chassis list rather than on an inference from generation. The A9K pair's contract names all seven chassis; the A99 pair's names five - "ASR 9922, ASR 9912, ASR 9910, ASR 9906 and ASR 9904" - so the two are not interchangeable even though they share an envelope. A component that declares what it fits is a better source than a chassis deciding what it will take","four-port-100ge":"datasheet - c78-740092's "Chassis compatibility" row: "Compatible with the Cisco ASR 9006, ASR 9010, ASR 9904, ASR 9906, ASR 9910, ASR 9912, and ASR 9922 chassis". All seven, stated outright, and the component's own attrs.chassis carries the same list. At 41.4 mm it fits every line card bay in the family. Added to the line card slots only - a compatibility row names a chassis, not a slot, and this chassis's RSP and RP positions take supervisors","grounding":"datasheet - "Bottom rear right side of the chassis", b-asr9k-hardware-installation-guide.pdf p125, illustrated by Figure 137","lifecycle":"datasheet - searched. No end-of-sale or end-of-life notice for this chassis was found","master-faces-verified":"drawing - checked deliberately, because Cisco's ASR 9910 masters are SWAPPED and modelling from a filename there would build the chassis inside out. The 9912's are correctly named: asr-9912-ac-front carries the cable management tray with the cisco logo, both card cages and the populated power shelves, while asr-9912-ac-rear carries the two fan trays, a block of yellow warning labels and the power inlets. Figure 23 corroborates by marking the fan trays "(rear insertion)"","no-chassis-power-figure":"NOTE, and NARROWED. The current Table 14 says only to use the Cisco Power Calculator, so there is no chassis-level figure for THIS chassis in any document held, and the module total here is a floor. That is narrower than what an earlier revision of this file claimed: it said Cisco publishes no chassis draw for ANY ASR 9000, and that is false. The older Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide (asr9kELCIGbk.pdf, OL-17500-09) states "Power Dissipation 7600 W maximum (Cisco ASR 9010 Router)" and 4556 W maximum for the ASR 9006 in its Table A-1 - a table the current revision deleted. Those two chassis predate this one and no equivalent figure for this model appears in either revision, so this is the vendor being silent about this chassis rather than about the family","pitch-against-the-siblings":"NOTE - 44.06 here against 43.78 measured the same way on the ASR 9910 and 43.75 on the ASR 9906. The 0.28 mm difference is larger than either chassis's own label spread, so it is probably real rather than noise, and it is consistent with the 9912 and 9922 being a slightly different mechanical build from the 9906 and 9910 - they take the full-width A99-SFC3 fabric card at 41.4 mm where the 9910 takes the double-width A99-SFC3-S at 76.2. Recorded rather than averaged away","power-shelves-derived-from-a-neighbour":"DERIVED, not measured, and the derivation is better than the estimate it replaces. The three shelves were placed by eye at y 1125, 1195 and 1265 because the master draws them populated and no separator rule is readable. That estimate put shelf-0 ELEVEN MILLIMETRES INSIDE the RP bay: the RP/FC cage ends at 1117.36 and an RP bay carries 18.77 mm of ejector past it, so nothing can begin above 1136.13. That is a constraint from a part with nothing to do with power. Three shelves then fill 1136.13 to the chassis bottom at 1333.50 - 197.37 mm, 65.79 each - and are placed at 1136.50, 1202.17 and 1267.84 on a 65.67 pitch at 63.0 tall, which leaves a visible gap between them and lands the last edge 0.66 mm short of the chassis bottom. THE TWO DECIMAL PLACES ARE ARITHMETIC AND NOT PRECISION. The underlying inputs are a measured cage edge and a published ejector allowance; nothing in any figure resolves a power shelf to a hundredth of a millimetre. Read them as "three shelves evenly filling the space the RP bay leaves", which is what they are","ru":"datasheet - 52.5 in / 1.75 = exactly 30.00 RU, and the stencil's height_in of 5.2500 agrees exactly. One of the four chassis in the family where the guide and the stencil need no reconciling","side-and-top-faces":"datasheet - NAMED but not dimensioned, and drawn as regions rather than decor for that reason. Figure 14 (the chassis footprint figure in b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf) shows the top plate outline and the rack mounting brackets, and Figure 77 (the chassis cooling path side view) shows the airflow through the side. Both name what is on those faces; NEITHER dimensions any feature on them, so nothing here carries coordinates. Contrast the ASR 9906, whose HIG Figure 17 gives explicit rail positions at 9.45 in and 5.00 in from the rear and where those rails ARE drawn. The distinction is deliberate: a region says "this is here" and decor says "this is here, at this size, in this place", and only the second needs a dimension behind it","side-face-labels-say-when-a-position-is-UNKNOWN":"every region on a side face now states either where the feature sits or that no figure dimensions it. That second half is the point. A region reading only "Vertical rack rail locations" is silent about position, and silence is indistinguishable from a position that was known and not written down - which is exactly how a feature ends up drawn at the wrong end with nothing to contradict it. casa-cards found seven such features across two chassis where the LABEL WAS RIGHT AND THE GEOMETRY WAS WRONG, and lint stayed green because no rule compares the two. Saying "present but not dimensioned" gives a reader the same thing a distance would: a claim to check the drawing against","slot-pitch-measured-from-the-card-guide-rails":"measured - CORRECTED. An earlier revision of this file said both cages PRINT their positions. They do not: what was measured is the row of bolt heads on each cage's card guide rail, checked by eye at 2400 px after the same reading was found to be wrong on the ASR 9910. The numbers are unchanged, because a uniform rail is a better ruler than printed text - a label's centre moves with its character count, and on the 9910 the text row gives pitches ranging 41.78 to 55.16 where its rail gives 43.78 with a spread of 0.2. Ten line card rail bolts centre at 25.08 through 421.61 mm with nine pitches of 44.10, 43.99, 44.09, 44.09, 43.99, 44.10, 44.09, 43.99 and 44.09 - a mean of 44.06 with a spread of 0.11 mm. The nine RP/FC positions give the same 44.05, so the two cages share a pitch, which is what makes a fabric card and a line card the same mechanical slot here. Both cages measure 6.36 to 440.24 mm across the body. THE SIBLING CONFIRMS IT: the ASR 9922's front master, measured the same way, gives 44.06 with a spread of 0.11 - identical, and the two are the same build","slots":"datasheet - Figure 23 "Cisco ASR 9912 Router Slot Numbering", p38 of b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf, read at 250 dpi. Top to bottom: fan trays FT0 over FT1 marked "rear insertion"; then Slot 0 to Slot 9 carrying LC0 to LC9; then a second cage of nine positions labelled by NAME and not by slot number - RP0, FC0, FC1, FC2, FC3, FC4, FC5, FC6, RP1; then power shelves PS0, PS1, PS2 each M0 to M3. The RP/FC positions are named directly by Cisco, so they are named directly here rather than given invented slot numbers","strip-is-centred-on-the-plane":"the rack mounting strip is 3.9 mm thick and is placed so the DIMENSIONED PLANE PASSES THROUGH ITS MIDDLE, at y = plane - 1.95. Neither edge carries the number. An earlier revision put the plane on one edge, which meant the figure's dimension was 3.9 mm from where the drawing said it was, and which edge differed between chassis - casa-cards found the same inconsistency across the two it owns and centred them the same way","strip-label-carries-the-number":"the region label states the figure's own dimension AND its conversion to a distance from the front. That is not decoration: it is the only number in the file a reader can check the geometry against, and its absence is why the ASR 9906's strips sat in the wrong half of the box through two reviews before a human noticed. Where the label carried a distance - on the ASR 9006 and 9904 - the same error was caught in minutes","top-and-bottom-agree":"the rack mounting flange is one vertical plate, so it intersects the top and bottom planes at the SAME depth and appears on both faces at the same y. An earlier revision drew it only on the bottom, which left the two faces of one chassis disagreeing about where the chassis bolts to the rack - the kind of internal inconsistency this work has spent the night finding in other people's artefacts. casa-cards' ASR 9006 and 9904 match across both faces and are the standard this follows","top-and-bottom-view-convention":"ON THIS CHASSIS'S TOP AND BOTTOM VIEWS, y = 0 IS THE REAR AND y = depth IS THE FRONT. Verified on this chassis's own footprint figure rather than carried across from a sibling: the figure prints "Rear of chassis" above the drawing and "Front of chassis" below it, read by eye because that text is vector art and does not extract. Stated here because it is not derivable from the file and because reading it the other way turns every depth-wise position into its complement - which is exactly the error that put this family's ASR 9906 strips in the wrong half of the box.","twelve-port-100ge":"datasheet - c78-737623's "Chassis compatibility" row reads "Compatible with the Cisco ASR 9904, ASR 9910, ASR 9912, and ASR 9922 chassis". This chassis is named, so cisco/a99-12x100ge@1 joins the line card bays. NOTE WHICH CHASSIS IS ABSENT: the ASR 9906. That card goes in every other 9900-generation chassis and not in the 9906, which is the second time a Cisco compatibility row has singled that chassis out, and exactly why these lists are transcribed rather than inferred from generation","weight":"datasheet - Table 13.
